title: Why Europe Sailed West
description: Economic motives, crusading ideology, maritime technology, Columbus's miscalculation, and the 1494 treaty division of the world between Spain and Portugal: the causes of European exploration.
essential_question: Why did European rulers spend money on voyages into an unknown ocean?
learning_objectives: Explain the economic pressures that pushed Iberian rulers to seek a western route to Asia.
Describe how the Reconquista and new maritime technology made sustained Atlantic voyages possible.
Rank the motives of gold, God, and glory and justify the hierarchy with evidence.

key_terms.definition: The centuries-long Christian reconquest of Iberia from Muslim rule, completed with the fall of Granada in 1492.
A small, fast Portuguese sailing ship with lateen sails capable of sailing against the wind on long Atlantic voyages.
The 1494 treaty between Spain and Portugal dividing newly discovered lands: west of the line to Spain, east of the line to Portugal.

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: [beat]Columbus was wrong about almost everything. His math shrank the Earth to make Asia look like a short sail west. The experts checked his numbers and said no. [beat] Spain paid for the voyage anyway. Three small ships, into the unmapped Atlantic. Why would a king and queen fund a plan the experts rejected?

narration.text: [solemn]Start with hunger. Not for food. For pepper. After the Crusades, Europe craved Asian spices, silk, and perfumes. But every bale traveled overland through Islamic powers and Italian city-states, and each middleman took a cut. By the time the goods reached Lisbon, prices had multiplied. [beat] A sea route straight to Asia would skip every taxman. Whoever found it would command the richest trade on Earth.

narration.text: [beat]Portugal moved first. In the mid-1400s, Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored voyage after voyage down the coast of Africa. The tool was the caravel, a small Portuguese ship with lateen sails that could tack against the wind, guided by the astrolabe and compass. [beat] In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope. A decade later, Vasco da Gama reached India. Portugal built its sea route one careful voyage at a time. narration.text: [fierce:1.2]Spain came late, because Spain was busy. For nearly eight centuries, Christian kingdoms fought the Reconquista, retaking Iberia from Muslim rule. In 1492, Granada fell. The war was over. Spain stood united under Ferdinand and Isabella, holding a crusading army with nowhere left to march. [beat] That crusading spirit did not retire. It turned outward: strike at Islam's flank, carry the faith across the ocean, win glory doing it.

narration.text: [beat]Enter Columbus: a Genoese sailor with a wrong map and a gift for persuasion. He argued the Earth was smaller than the experts said, which put Asia within reach. He asked Portugal first. Portugal, confident in its African route, turned him down. [beat] Then he asked Spain. Ferdinand and Isabella had just united the country and were flush with victory. The price was tiny: three small ships. On October 12, 1492, he sighted land, an island he named San Salvador, and called its people Indians. He believed he had reached Asia.

narration.text: So why did they sail? The textbooks answer: gold, God, and glory. [beat] Look at the three. Which one actually paid for the ships? [pause:2] Gold. Follow the money. Portugal spent fifty years mapping Africa for trade, not converts. Columbus pitched the treasures of the East. Spain and Portugal divided the planet by treaty to lock up their claims. [beat] God mattered. The crusading zeal was real, and missionaries sailed with every flag. Glory mattered. Crowns competed, and explorers won titles. But neither launched one ship without the promise of profit. [emphasis]Gold first.[/emphasis] God and glory rode along.
